claims.claim: The work is attributed to 'Hesychius, priest of Jerusalem' (πρεσβυτέρου Ἱεροσολύμων), but this attribution is disputed and considered a misattribution.
The work is not by the fifth-century Hesychius of Jerusalem, but by a different or later author.
The work was possibly written in the 6th century or later.
The work was probably written in Cappadocia, or perhaps in Palestine.
The work recounts the legend of Longinus, the centurion who attended the crucifixion of Christ and believed in him.

In the legend, Longinus was initially tortured under King Herod of Judaea for confessing the newly-born Christ as God, lived until Christ's crucifixion, attended it, and was later martyred at the village of Andralis near Tyana in Cappadocia.
A shrine was founded at Longinus's martyrdom site after the recovery of his head from Jerusalem by a widow.
The work is preserved in abridged form in tenth-century Synaxaria.
The work is also known as Homily 20, Encomium on Longinus, and has the CPG number 6590 and BHG number 990.
The work was edited by M. Aubineau in 'Les homélies festales d'Hésychius de Jérusalem, Vol. 2. Les homélies xvi-xxi (Subsidia hagiographica 59)', Brussels, 1980, pages 872-901.
The author is referred to as 'Pseudo-Hesychius of Jerusalem' in modern scholarship due to the disputed attribution.
